source.title: SS-SAM : Stochastic Scheduled Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Training Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Yang Zhao; Hao Zhang; Xiuyuan Hu

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper. Its title in the text differs from the catalog title; the arXiv identifier matches.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains models with sharpness-aware and gradient-norm regularization methods and reports held-out error, but does not measure the train–test gap or test any mapped version's specific claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-error results for SGD/SAM and randomized or generalized randomized sharpness-aware training (RST/G-RST), including changes across schedules. These results concern test performance, but do not report training error, memorization of random labels, width sweeps, convolution-versus-fully-connected comparisons, adaptive-optimizer comparisons, batch-size sweeps, dropout, magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, or example removal.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima generalize better to develop efficient sharpness-aware training. Its results compare method test errors and computation costs; they do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap association or any other listed version. Adam is used for ViTs and SGD for CNNs, without a controlled comparison between them.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that RST reduces sharpness-aware training overhead and that G-RST can outperform SAM while halving its extra computation. This concerns additional overhead, not total training cost, and improvement is not universal in Tables 3 and 4.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies randomized mixtures of SGD/SAM and SGD/gradient-norm regularization; its outcomes are test error and computation cost, not the mapped claim's train–test-gap measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Test error varies with the RST scheduling function and its probability over training; the authors report that frequent SGD selection near the end harms performance. G-RST outcomes also vary by model and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Tables 3 and 4 report lower mean test errors for SAM and G-RST than their base optimizers. G-RST has lower mean error than SAM in most comparisons, but higher error for VGG16BN/CIFAR-100 (24.37 versus 24.23) and ViT-B16/CIFAR-10 (5.58 versus 5.45).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Randomized sharpness-aware training can retain or improve held-out classification performance while reducing the additional computation of SAM, with outcomes depending on model, dataset, and schedule.

record.problems: The reported generalization results are test errors, not train–test gaps. The text does not report training errors or memorization capacity. Most reported settings average five seeds; ImageNet table results use three seeds. No uncertainty measure for any gap is available.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional schedule-specific curves and tables, cutout results, and results for SAM variants and efficiency techniques. They are omitted because the 60-row limit prioritizes distinct model, dataset, and method results in Tables 3 and 4; the additional schedule and appendix comparisons are not needed to represent the same test-error outcomes.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting and held-out performance under natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error and resulting test-error trends.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and effects of tuning or optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons within a workload under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with measured train–test gaps, and comparison against norm- and margin-based measures. Neither SAM performance nor ASAM performance measures this association.
Removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked to V1–V8 and should be retained only as findings outside those versions. The record's fits_no_version summary misses the VGG16BN/CIFAR-100 exception. Excerpt E4 concerns low selection probabilities in Appendix B.2, not an explanation established for r26's fixed p=0.5 result.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Width sweep past interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparisons under tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout comparisons and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its association with train–test gap; the paper compares sharpness-aware training outcomes but does not measure this property or gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

relation.reason: Sharpness-aware generalization motivates the method; the experiments compare training schemes without measuring the association specified by V7 or testing another listed version.

tranche.reason: The study uses the flat-minima premise to develop efficient training and reports method test errors and computation costs. It does not test any listed claim version, including V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap association.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv:2203.09962v2 (April 2023), titled Randomized Sharpness-Aware Training for Boosting Computational Efficiency in Deep Learning; the pack uses a different title and 2022 year. Table 3 gives WRN28-10/CIFAR-100 SGD error 18.99±0.12, whereas Table 1 gives 18.69±0.12; the listed rows correctly follow Table 3.
